questions.q: Name the 9th-century Persian scholar who wrote *Kitab al-Jam' wa'l-Tafriq bi Hisab al-Hind* (Book of Addition and Subtraction According to the Hindu Calculation), which systematically explained the Hindu numeral system to the Islamic world.
questions.a: Al-Khwarizmi (c. 780–850 CE). A wrong answer like "Al-Biruni" or "Omar Khayyam" reveals confusion between scholars who transmitted Indian mathematics (Al-Khwarizmi, Al-Kindi) and later Persian polymaths who built on it. Students may also confuse Al-Khwarizmi with the later Fibonacci who brought the system to Europe.

questions.q: Why did the Hindu-Arabic numeral system spread more rapidly in the Islamic world than in India itself during the 8th-10th centuries?
questions.a: The Abbasid Caliphate actively sponsored translation movements in Baghdad's House of Wisdom, creating a unified scholarly language (Arabic) across a vast empire from Spain to Central Asia. Indian texts arrived in a context of thriving trade, tax administration, and astronomy that demanded efficient calculation. A wrong answer focusing only on "Arab traders liked it" misses the institutional support (caliphal patronage, madrasas, shared language) that enabled systematic adoption and adaptation.

questions.q: A merchant in 1200 CE Pisa wants to multiply 347 × 268. Using Roman numerals (CCCXLVII × CCLXVIII), explain why this is impractical compared to Hindu-Arabic numerals, and show the Hindu-Arabic multiplication step-by-step.
questions.a: Roman numerals lack place value and zero, making written algorithms impossible — multiplication requires repeated addition or an abacus. Hindu-Arabic steps: (1) Write 347 × 268 vertically. (2) Multiply 347 × 8 = 2776. (3) Multiply 347 × 60 = 20820 (shift left). (4) Multiply 347 × 200 = 69400 (shift left twice). (5) Add: 2776 + 20820 + 69400 = 92,996. Wrong answers that attempt Roman multiplication reveal misunderstanding that Roman numerals are additive, not positional.

questions.q: Compare the roles of Al-Khwarizmi (c. 825 CE) and Fibonacci (1202 CE) in the transmission chain. How did their audiences and purposes differ?
questions.a: Al-Khwarizmi wrote in Arabic for Islamic scholars, administrators, and judges needing systematic arithmetic for inheritance, tax, and astronomy — his work was academic and legal. Fibonacci wrote *Liber Abaci* in Latin for European merchants and bankers, emphasising practical commercial problems (currency conversion, profit sharing, interest). A wrong answer treating both as "mathematicians spreading numbers" misses the shift from scholarly/legal context to commercial/mercantile context that drove European adoption.

questions.q: A student claims: "Europeans adopted Hindu-Arabic numerals immediately after Fibonacci's *Liber Abaci* in 1202 because they were clearly better." Evaluate this claim with historical evidence.
questions.a: The claim is false. Adoption took 300+ years (1202–1500s). Resistance came from: (1) Church suspicion of "Arabic" symbols, (2) entrenched abacus/counting-board guilds, (3) Roman numerals' adequacy for record-keeping (not calculation), (4) lack of printing press until 1450. *Liber Abaci* circulated in manuscript; printed arithmetic books (e.g., Treviso Arithmetic 1478) accelerated adoption. Wrong answers ignoring institutional inertia reveal a "great man" view of history rather than systemic change.

questions.q: Design a museum exhibit panel (150 words) showing the evolution of the digit '5' from Brahmi (3rd century BCE) → Gupta (4th century CE) → Arabic (9th century) → Medieval European (12th century) → Modern printed form. Explain one shape change at each stage.
questions.a: A good answer traces: Brahmi '5' as two horizontal strokes (≡) → Gupta cursive joins them into a loop with tail → Arabic *khamsa* rotates 90° and opens the loop → European manuscripts add a top stroke for clarity → printing standardises the top horizontal and closed lower loop. Poor answers list shapes without explaining *why* (cursive writing, rotation in right-to-left script, differentiation from '6', printing constraints), showing rote memorisation without understanding material causes of script evolution.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The ______ of Hindu numerals refers to the historical process by which the Indian decimal place-value system with zero (0-9) spread from India to the Islamic world (8th-12th centuries CE) through scholars like Al-Khwarizmi and Al-Kindi, and then to Europe (10th-15th centuries CE) via translations in Spain and Italy, replacing Roman numerals and enabling modern arithmetic.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you're a ______ in 12th century Pisa trying to calculate profits from trade with Egypt using Roman numerals — you'd need an abacus and hours of work.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you're a merchant in ______th century Pisa trying to calculate profits from trade with Egypt using Roman numerals — you'd need an abacus and hours of work.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Student can explain the key stages, figures, and routes of transmission from India to the Arab world to Europe, and articulate why the Hindu-Arabic system replaced Roman numerals for calculation.
